title: The Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958: Coverage, the Rent Threshold, and How Eviction Actually Works
subtitle: Why the 1958 Act, not its unenforced 1995 successor, still governs Delhi tenancies, and how Section 14 grounds, Section 25B summary eviction and the Transfer of Property Act route fit together
meta_description: How the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 applies today: the rent threshold, Section 14 eviction grounds, Section 25B procedure, and the civil route outside it.
author: Adv. Rahul Jangra, Chandrayee Roy
author_role: Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
standfirst: Most landlords and tenants in Delhi assume that any dispute over rent or possession lands before the Rent Controller, and are then surprised to learn that a large and growing share of the city's tenancies, once rent crosses a fixed threshold that has stayed unchanged since 1988, fall outside the Delhi Rent Control Act altogether and are fought instead as ordinary civil suits. This piece sets out who the Act actually covers, how an eviction petition under Section 14 proceeds, why the summary procedure under Section 25B decides most such cases faster than an ordinary suit would, and what changes once a tenancy sits outside the Act's protection.
key_points: The Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 remains the operative statute. A replacement Act passed by Parliament in 1995 received presidential assent but was never notified into force, so the 1958 Act, as amended in 1988, continues to govern Delhi tenancies.

Section 3 takes several categories of premises outside the Act entirely, the most consequential being premises, residential or commercial, where the monthly rent exceeds Rs 3,500, a threshold fixed by the 1988 amendment and upheld by the Supreme Court and never revised since.

Premises outside the Act are not rent-free zones; landlords sue for possession and arrears as an ordinary civil suit, typically after a notice to quit under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, rather than filing before the Rent Controller.

Within the Act, Section 14(1) lists specific grounds on which a landlord may seek eviction, from non-payment of rent to the landlord's own bona fide requirement to misuse of the premises, and a landlord confined to the Act cannot evict a tenant on a ground outside this list.

Most eviction petitions on specified grounds, including the bona fide requirement ground, are decided under the summary procedure in Section 25B, where the tenant must apply for leave to defend and show a genuine triable issue, failing which the petition's averments are treated as admitted.

A Rent Controller's order on leave to defend or on the eviction petition itself is tested before the Delhi High Court by way of revision under Section 25B(8), not by a regular first appeal, and the High Court's revisional jurisdiction in this setting is itself limited in scope.

Section 50 bars civil courts from matters that fall within the Rent Controller's jurisdiction, but that bar depends on the Act actually applying, so a dispute over whether rent lawfully crosses the Rs 3,500 threshold can itself become the first fight in the case.

sections.heading: A 1958 Act that has outlived its own replacement
paragraphs: Tenancies in Delhi are still governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, not because Parliament never tried to replace it, but because the replacement never actually took effect. The Delhi Rent Act, 1995 was passed by Parliament and received presidential assent in August 1995, and it was drafted to repeal the 1958 Act through its own Section 82. Under Section 1(3) of the 1995 Act, however, that repeal and the new Act's substantive provisions were to commence only on a date the Central Government notified, and that notification was never issued. A Lok Sabha answer on record confirms that the government decided to bring the 1995 Act into force only with amendments, and that it was, in its own words, not in a position to bring the Act as assented to into force. A writ petition seeking a mandamus to notify the Act was filed in the late 1990s, and more than two decades on, commentary on the subject as recent as 2025 continues to describe the 1958 Act, not its 1995 successor, as the operative law.

The practical upshot for anyone dealing with a Delhi tenancy today is straightforward: cite and apply the 1958 Act as amended, principally by the Delhi Rent Control (Amendment) Act, 1988, and treat the 1995 Act as a piece of unenforced legislation that occasionally comes up in argument but has no operative effect on an actual dispute. Advocates who are used to a different state's more recently enacted rent law should not assume Delhi has one too.

sections.heading: Who the Act actually covers, and the Rs 3,500 line
paragraphs: The Act's territorial reach is wide. Section 1(2) extends it to areas within the New Delhi Municipal Council, the Delhi Cantonment Board, and such urban areas within the Municipal Corporation of Delhi as are specified in the First Schedule, so premises in NDMC and cantonment areas fall squarely within the Act rather than outside it, and a newly developed MCD area needs its own notification under the proviso to Section 1(2) before the Act extends to it at all.

Section 3 then carves specific categories of premises out of the Act regardless of location. Premises belonging to the Government are excluded outright. Premises constructed on or after the 1988 amendment's commencement get a ten-year exemption from the date construction is completed, an incentive meant to encourage new rental housing stock. The exemption that drives the most litigation, however, is Section 3(c): premises, whether let for residential or non-residential use, where the rent payable exceeds Rs 3,500 a month, fall entirely outside the Act. The Supreme Court upheld this threshold against a constitutional challenge in D.C. Bhatia and Others versus Union of India, reported at (1995) 1 SCC 104, holding that the classification was not arbitrary and that the provision operates prospectively rather than disturbing proceedings already pending when it came into force.

The threshold has not moved since 1988, which means a very large and growing share of Delhi's rental stock, almost anything let at a realistic current market rent in most parts of the city, now sits outside the Act's protection by simple arithmetic rather than by any fresh policy choice. Courts have been firm that the relevant figure is the actual rent payable on the relevant date, not some notional or historic figure, and that maintenance or other charges bundled into the rent can be counted toward the threshold where they form part of what the tenant actually pays each month. A landlord who raises rent partway through a tenancy and crosses the threshold only from that point cannot treat the increase as reaching back to cover the period before it took effect; the increase operates prospectively, so whether the Act applied at any given moment during the tenancy depends on what was actually payable at that moment, not on the rent payable today.

The unenforced 1995 Act, for what it is worth, would have gone further still. Its own exemption provisions reportedly extended the carve-out to premises that had not been let out for seven years before a fresh letting, running for fifteen years from that letting, and brought local authorities within the same exclusion already applied to Government premises. None of that has any legal effect today, since the 1995 Act was never notified into force, but practitioners should be careful not to mistake its more liberal exemptions, sometimes quoted online without the context that the Act itself never commenced, for the law actually in force.

sections.heading: Outside the Act: the Transfer of Property Act route
paragraphs: A tenancy that falls outside the Act because of the rent threshold, because the premises are government-owned, or because the construction is still within its ten-year exemption window, does not become a lawless space. It simply moves out of the Rent Controller's jurisdiction and into the ordinary civil court system, governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and the Code of Civil Procedure rather than by the Act's special machinery. A landlord in this position terminates the tenancy by a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, typically a fifteen-day notice for a month-to-month tenancy of non-agricultural premises unless the lease itself fixes a different period, and then files a civil suit for possession and, if arrears are also due, for recovery of rent and mesne profits.

This route is slower in one sense, since a civil suit does not come with the Act's summary procedure, but it is also freer in another: a landlord suing outside the Act is not confined to the specific grounds listed in Section 14 and does not need to establish bona fide requirement, non-payment, or any of the other statutory grounds, because the suit proceeds on ordinary principles of contract and tenancy law. Courts have also recognised that where the Act's own rent-fixation or threshold machinery is in a genuine vacuum, for instance where a statutory provision fixing or testing the rent has itself been struck down or is otherwise inoperative, a civil suit for market rent can proceed notwithstanding the Act, rather than being stalled indefinitely while that vacuum is sorted out.

The dividing line is not always obvious at the time a landlord decides where to file, because whether the rent in fact exceeds Rs 3,500 can itself be disputed, particularly where a tenant argues that a purported rent increase was invalid or that charges being added to push the rent over the threshold do not actually count as rent. Where that question is live, courts have held that the civil court's jurisdiction depends on the Rent Controller first deciding whether the rent lawfully crosses the threshold, so a landlord confident that a tenancy sits outside the Act should expect that confidence to be tested as a preliminary issue rather than assumed away.

sections.heading: Inside the Act: standard rent and the grounds that matter
paragraphs: For tenancies the Act does cover, either the landlord or the tenant can apply to the Rent Controller under Section 9 to fix the standard rent under Section 6 or the permitted increase under Section 7, and the Controller is directed to fix a rent that is reasonable having regard to the circumstances of the case where the Act's own formula cannot be mechanically applied. An application for fixation generally proceeds in the prescribed form under the Delhi Rent Control Rules, 1959, and the Controller can fix an interim rent while the application is pending, so that a dispute over the correct figure does not leave the landlord without any rent at all in the interim.

Eviction, as distinct from rent fixation, is governed by Section 14, which as a general rule bars a landlord from recovering possession of any premises covered by the Act except on the specific grounds the section lists. Those grounds include non-payment of rent, subletting without the landlord's consent, the tenant's acquisition of alternative suitable accommodation, misuse of the premises for a purpose other than what was let, and, among the grounds added by later amendment, a landlord's bona fide requirement of residential premises for personal occupation or that of a dependent family member. A landlord who cannot bring the case within one of these specific grounds cannot obtain possession under Section 14 no matter how reasonable the request otherwise seems, which is why so much Section 14 litigation turns on whether the facts truly fit the pleaded ground rather than on the underlying fairness of the landlord's request.

sections.heading: Bona fide requirement: the most litigated ground
paragraphs: Clause (e) of the proviso to Section 14(1) lets a landlord seek eviction of residential premises genuinely needed for the landlord's own occupation or for a dependent family member's occupation, where the landlord has no other reasonably suitable accommodation available. Courts have treated this as a question of fact rather than a checklist, since the Act does not exhaustively define what counts as bona fide requirement, and decisions on the point are built up through case law rather than a fixed statutory test. What does recur across reported decisions is that once a landlord makes out a prima facie case of personal requirement, the Controller may proceed on a presumption that the need is bona fide, shifting the practical burden onto the tenant to show either that the claim is not genuine or that the landlord already has suitable alternative accommodation.

A landlord relying on this ground is not required to hold absolute title to the property; courts have accepted that an interest short of full ownership can support a bona fide requirement claim, provided the landlord's relationship to the property and to the family member on whose behalf occupation is sought is genuine. The ground is also available repeatedly rather than being exhausted by a single unsuccessful attempt, with the Delhi High Court having held that the pendency of an earlier eviction petition between the same parties does not prevent the landlord from filing a fresh petition on a different ground, including a later-arising bona fide requirement. What a landlord cannot do is use a bona fide requirement petition to recover non-residential premises; the Supreme Court has held that the scheme of the Act does not permit recovery of premises let for non-residential purposes on this ground, which is confined to residential premises.

sections.heading: Section 25B: why most eviction petitions move faster than ordinary suits
paragraphs: Eviction petitions on the specified grounds that Section 25B names, bona fide requirement prominent among them, are decided under a summary procedure rather than as an ordinary trial, and this is the single biggest practical difference between litigating under the Act and litigating a comparable dispute as a civil suit. Once such a petition is filed, the tenant is served with a summons in the form the Third Schedule prescribes and must apply for leave to defend, supported by an affidavit, within the period that schedule fixes; if no such application is made in time, the petition's averments are treated as admitted and the Controller can pass an eviction order without a contested hearing at all.

Where the tenant does apply, the standard for deciding whether to grant leave was set out by the Supreme Court in Precision Steel and Engineering Works versus Prem Deva Niranjan Deva Tayal and has been applied consistently since: the tenant need not prove the defence at this stage, only show a triable issue, meaning a defence that, if established, could lead to dismissal of the eviction petition. A wholly frivolous or moonshine defence will not clear this bar, and a leave application lacking any credible triable issue is liable to be dismissed outright, but a genuine, specifically pleaded dispute of fact ordinarily entitles the tenant to a contested hearing rather than summary eviction. Whether a tenant's delay in filing the leave application can itself be condoned has divided Rent Controllers and even benches of the High Court; one line of authority treats the Limitation Act as inapplicable to this specific timeline and therefore not condonable, while another finds nothing in Section 25B itself that forecloses condonation, and the point was still being referred to a larger bench in some of the material available at the time of writing, so a tenant who has missed the deadline should not assume either outcome and should apply for leave, with an explanation for the delay, at the earliest possible moment rather than treating the point as settled.

sections.heading: Challenging the outcome: revision, not a regular appeal
paragraphs: A party aggrieved by the Controller's order, whether refusing leave to defend, granting it, or deciding the eviction petition itself, does not get an ordinary first appeal. The proviso to Section 25B(8) instead gives the Delhi High Court a revisional jurisdiction over such orders, and the Supreme Court's own examination of how that power should be exercised confirms that it is a distinct, narrower jurisdiction rather than a rehearing of the merits as an appellate court would conduct one. In practice this means a tenant or landlord seeking to challenge an adverse order under Section 25B needs to frame the challenge around jurisdictional error, a failure to apply the correct legal standard such as the Precision Steel triable-issue test, or a result that is perverse on the material on record, rather than simply re-arguing the facts in the hope of a different outcome on reappraisal.

The Delhi High Court has also made clear that a landlord cannot use an appeal or revision under this scheme to expand the eviction petition beyond the ground actually pleaded before the Controller. A petition filed and argued on the bona fide requirement ground under clause (e), for instance, cannot be rescued on revision by invoking a different clause of Section 14(1) that was never pleaded in the first place, since the tenant must have had a fair opportunity to meet the specific case actually made against them.

sections.heading: Section 50 and the limits of the civil court's role
paragraphs: Section 50(1) bars civil courts from entertaining any suit or proceeding over a matter that the Act places within the Rent Controller's jurisdiction, and the bar has been read broadly enough to catch disputes that are not framed as rent or eviction claims in form but amount to the same thing in substance, such as a tenant's suit to restrain a landlord from cutting off amenities, which one Delhi High Court ruling held fell within the bar and was accordingly liable to rejection under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

This bar is not absolute, and its two most important limits map onto points already covered above. First, the bar presupposes that the Act applies to the premises at all, so a dispute over whether the rent in fact exceeds the Rs 3,500 threshold can itself require the Rent Controller's determination before a civil court's jurisdiction is settled one way or the other, and at least one Delhi High Court decision has set aside a civil decree passed before that threshold question was resolved. Second, where the statutory machinery that would otherwise occupy the field, such as a provision for fixing or revising rent, has itself been struck down and no replacement mechanism exists, a resulting vacuum can take a dispute outside the practical reach of the bar, since there is no Rent Controller jurisdiction left for the bar to protect. Litigants on either side of a Delhi tenancy dispute should treat the choice between the Rent Controller and the civil court as a genuine threshold question to be analysed on the specific facts, not a formality to be assumed from the premises' general character.

sections.heading: Non-payment of rent and the tenant's chance to pay up
paragraphs: The most common ground pleaded under Section 14(1) is plain non-payment of rent, under clause (a) of the proviso. Even here the Act does not let a landlord move straight to eviction the moment an instalment is missed. Section 14(2) gives a tenant sued on this ground a statutory opportunity to make good the default, generally by depositing the arrears along with interest and costs as the Controller directs, and a tenant who complies within the time allowed is protected from eviction on that particular default even though the rent was, in fact, paid late. This protection against the first default is not unlimited; a tenant who has already taken the benefit of this provision once in respect of the same tenancy cannot keep relying on it for every subsequent default, and a landlord who shows a pattern of chronic default can eventually succeed on the non-payment ground despite a tenant's repeated last-minute deposits.

Running alongside the non-payment ground is Section 15, which lets the Controller direct a tenant contesting any eviction petition, regardless of the ground pleaded, to deposit arrears and ongoing rent during the pendency of the proceedings. Section 15(7) allows the Controller to strike out the tenant's defence on non-compliance, but the Supreme Court has held this power to be discretionary rather than automatic, to be exercised where the default in depositing is wilful or contumacious rather than for every missed or delayed deposit with a reasonable explanation. Tenants should not, however, treat that discretion as a safety net; Controllers who find a pattern of repeated, unexplained non-payment under a Section 15 order have had the defence struck out, and that order upheld, often enough that ongoing rent deposits during the litigation should be treated as a serious, parallel obligation rather than an afterthought.

sections.heading: Once an order is passed: execution, stay and appeal timelines
paragraphs: An eviction order under Section 14 is not immediately followed by forcible dispossession. Section 14(6) and the related provisions give the Controller discretion to allow the tenant a period of time to vacate, and that period is commonly used to negotiate a final settlement even after the legal contest has effectively been decided. Where the tenant wishes to challenge the order further, the correct route, as already discussed, is revision to the Delhi High Court under the proviso to Section 25B(8) rather than a regular appeal, and a tenant seeking to stay execution pending that revision needs to apply for interim protection specifically, since the filing of a revision petition does not by itself suspend the Controller's order.

For landlords, the flip side is that an eviction order obtained after a fully contested Section 25B proceeding is usually close to final in practical terms, because the revisional jurisdiction available to a tenant at that stage is deliberately narrow and does not offer the kind of fresh merits review that an ordinary first appeal would. This is precisely why the leave to defend stage, discussed earlier, carries so much weight in practice: it is realistically the tenant's best and sometimes only opportunity to have the underlying facts properly tested before a court, rather than one stage among several roughly equal opportunities to contest the case.

sections.heading: Practical guidance for landlords and tenants
paragraphs: A landlord planning to recover possession should start by establishing, on paper, whether the tenancy is covered by the Act at all. If the current rent exceeds Rs 3,500 a month, the premises are government-owned, or the building is still within its ten-year exemption from completion, the correct route is very likely a Section 106 notice followed by a civil suit, not a petition before the Rent Controller, and filing in the wrong forum invites delay rather than saving time. If the Act does apply, the landlord should identify, before filing, exactly which Section 14(1) ground the facts support, since the petition will be judged against that specific ground and cannot later be rescued by switching to a different one on appeal or revision.

A tenant served with an eviction petition under the Act should treat the leave to defend stage as the real contest, not a formality to be handled after the fact. Missing the window to apply, or filing an affidavit that does little more than deny the landlord's case in general terms without pointing to specific, triable facts, is the single most common way tenants lose cases that might otherwise have gone to a full hearing. Equally, a tenant should not assume that paying rent faithfully forecloses every ground of eviction; bona fide requirement, misuse and subletting are each independent grounds that have nothing to do with whether rent has been paid, and a tenant's defence needs to address the ground actually pleaded rather than the tenancy's history generally.

conclusion: The Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 continues to govern the city's tenancies only because its intended replacement was never switched on, a quirk of legislative history that practitioners dealing with Delhi property need to keep straight when a client assumes a newer law applies. Within the Act, the structure is reasonably settled: specific grounds under Section 14, a summary procedure under Section 25B for most of them, and a revisional rather than appellate check by the Delhi High Court on the outcome.

The harder judgment calls now sit at the Act's edges rather than at its centre, chiefly in deciding whether a given tenancy has in fact crossed the Rs 3,500 rent threshold and so moved outside the Act's protection altogether, and in working out which forum, the Rent Controller or the civil court, actually has jurisdiction when that question is itself disputed. Getting that threshold question right at the outset avoids the far costlier mistake of litigating an eviction or a civil suit for years in the wrong forum.

faqs.q: Does the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 still apply, or has it been replaced?
faqs.a: It still applies. The Delhi Rent Act, 1995 was passed by Parliament and received presidential assent, but it was never brought into force by the central government notification that its own commencement clause requires, so its repeal of the 1958 Act never took effect. The 1958 Act, as amended in 1988, remains the operative law.

faqs.q: Is my tenancy covered by the Act if the rent is above Rs 3,500 a month?
faqs.a: No. Section 3(c), inserted by the 1988 amendment and upheld by the Supreme Court in D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India, takes any premises, residential or commercial, outside the Act once the monthly rent exceeds Rs 3,500. Such tenancies are governed by the Transfer of Property Act and ordinary civil law instead.

faqs.q: What is the usual first step for a landlord to evict a tenant whose rent exceeds the Act's threshold?
faqs.a: A notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, followed, if the tenant does not vacate, by an ordinary civil suit for possession and, where arrears exist, for recovery of rent and mesne profits. The landlord is not confined to the grounds listed in Section 14 for this kind of suit.

faqs.q: On what grounds can a landlord evict a tenant under the Delhi Rent Control Act?
faqs.a: Section 14(1) lists specific grounds, including non-payment of rent, subletting without consent, the tenant's acquisition of alternative accommodation, misuse of the premises, and, for residential premises, the landlord's bona fide requirement for personal occupation or for a dependent family member. A landlord must bring the case within one of these grounds; there is no general discretionary ground for eviction under the Act.

faqs.q: What happens if a tenant does not apply for leave to defend an eviction petition in time?
faqs.a: Under Section 25B(4), the eviction petition's averments are treated as admitted, and the Rent Controller can pass an order for eviction without a contested hearing. Whether a late application can still be entertained is disputed in the case law, so a tenant who has missed the deadline should apply immediately with a clear explanation rather than assume the point is settled either way.

faqs.q: Can a tenant get a full trial to contest an eviction petition?
faqs.a: Only by first obtaining leave to defend, which the Controller grants where the tenant shows a genuine triable issue under the standard set in Precision Steel and Engineering Works v. Prem Deva Niranjan Deva Tayal. A bare denial without specific, triable facts does not meet this standard and usually results in leave being refused.

faqs.q: Where does a challenge to a Rent Controller's eviction order go?
faqs.a: To the Delhi High Court, by way of revision under the proviso to Section 25B(8), not as a regular first appeal. The High Court's revisional jurisdiction in this setting is narrower than an appeal and generally focuses on jurisdictional error or a failure to apply the correct legal standard rather than a fresh reappraisal of the facts.

faqs.q: Can a civil court hear a dispute that is really about rent or eviction?
faqs.a: Generally no. Section 50(1) bars civil courts from matters within the Rent Controller's jurisdiction under the Act. The bar does not apply, however, where the Act itself does not cover the premises, such as where rent exceeds the Rs 3,500 threshold, or where that threshold question is itself disputed and has not yet been decided by the Rent Controller.

verification_notes: WebFetch to primary and secondary legal sites (delhihighcourt.nic.in, mondaq.com, advocatekhoj.com) was blocked by this session's network policy throughout this run, so verification relies on WebSearch results that quote and attribute passages from these sites, cross-checked across independent results for every substantive fact. That the Delhi Rent Act, 1995 was assented to but never notified into force is confirmed from three independent lines: a Lok Sabha answer on record, a Casemine summary of the 1995 Act's own commencement clause, and a 2025 Drishti IAS analysis treating the 1958 Act as currently operative, with a 1997 writ petition confirming the gap was litigated at the time. The Rs 3,500 threshold under Section 3(c), its 1988 amendment origin, and its constitutional upholding in D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India, (1995) 1 SCC 104, are each confirmed from at least two independent case-law aggregators (Casemine, Courtkutchehry, Indian Kanoon mirrors) quoting the same statutory and judicial text; the amending Act's own number is reported inconsistently across sources (52 of 1988 in some, 57 of 1988 in others) and is therefore not stated as a specific Act number in the article. The Section 25B leave-to-defend standard from Precision Steel and Engineering Works v. Prem Deva Niranjan Deva Tayal is confirmed from multiple Delhi High Court decisions quoting and applying it; the exact fifteen-day period for filing the leave application sits in the Third Schedule rather than in the operative text of Section 25B itself, as one High Court decision notes, and is described accordingly rather than as a figure drawn directly from Section 25B. Whether delay in filing a leave application can be condoned is reported as genuinely unsettled, with Satpal Singh cited for one view and other Delhi High Court decisions for the contrary view, and is presented in the article as disputed rather than settled, consistent with STRICT_VERIFICATION. The full clause-by-clause list of Section 14(1) grounds beyond (a), (b), (e), (hh) and (k) could not be independently confirmed from the primary text in this run and is accordingly described only in general terms rather than with a complete clause list. The first-default protection under Section 14(2) and the discretionary, wilful-default standard for striking out a defence under Section 15(7), including Rajbir Singh v. Mohan Lal Sharma, are each confirmed from at least two independent case-law aggregators (Indian Kanoon mirrors and a Casemine analysis) quoting consistent passages; one Supreme Court-level excerpt in the search results used more mandatory language for Section 15(7), and that tension is flagged in the article rather than resolved, consistent with STRICT_VERIFICATION. No case is cited that was not independently returned, quoted and attributed by a WebSearch call opened in this run.
